newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. deadlocked on Iraqi plane; setback for U.S..
newsitem.headline: U.N. deadlocked on Iraqi plane; setback for U.S..

text.p: In an apparent setback for the United States, the Security Council late on Friday failed to agree on a statement about whether an Iraqi pilgrim flight to Saudi Arabia violated U.N. sanctions.
Washington's chief representative, Bill Richardson, told reporters that after hours of discussion the council would have to resume its talks again on Monday.
A Chinese spokesman said his government did not believe that the Iraqi action violated sanctions.

"Progress is being made, discussions are going to continue," Richardson said. "It is our very strong view that an incident like this should not be repeated. We are working with council members to make sure this doesn't happen."
"We remain behind the view that this is a violation," he added, saying that a majority of the council agreed with him, "but there are still some delicate matters that have to be dealt with."
But some diplomats noted that while China was opposed to any statement, other countries objected to a strong one.
A late Friday night compromise draft was so weak that Richardson refused to endorse it, they said.
At issue is a flight on Wednesday from Baghdad to Jeddah and back taking 104 pilgrims on the annual haj.

U.N. legal counsel, Under-Secretary-General Hans Corell of Sweden, has told council members that Gulf War resolutions barring Iraqi flights were not as clear-cut as those imposed on Libya in 1992 in connection with the 1988 bombing of a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland, envoys said.

But he was also quoted as saying that, on the basis of past committee practice, Iraq did require advance permission for such flights. Committee sources said Iraq had itself acknowleged this by requesting permission in the past, although the committee had refused to grant it.

One version of the statement would also remind other countries, in this case Saudi Arabia, of their obligations under the sanctions, which require denial of overflight permission for unauthorised Iraqi aircraft and the impounding of any that nonetheless landed in their territory.
Some envoys quipped that Corell's explanation appeared to make it legal for Iraq to fly an aircraft, but not to land it without running the risk of losing the plane.
Consensus among all members is required before the council can issue a statement. If this cannot be reached, the issue could be made the subject of a resolution and put to a vote next week.
